seasons.review_body: Belascoaran, PI is one of the more quietly assured crime shows Netflix Mexico has produced: three feature-length episodes, each adapted from a different Paco Ignacio Taibo II novel, set in 1970s Mexico City with a visual palette that commits fully to the era. Luis Gerardo Mendez plays Hector Belascoaran with the off-balance charm of a man who has no idea what he is doing but keeps going anyway - which is precisely the joke and the point. The show blends detective procedural with deadpan comedy in proportions that critics found effective. Rotten Tomatoes registered 88 percent (2 critics), with Decider calling it stylish and fast-moving. IMDb audience scores confirmed broad approval at 7.3. The three-episode format, each case self-contained and feature-length, gives the show an anthology quality that suits the source material.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Belascoaran Pi S01E01: "Days in Combat" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The name lands before the man does. "Belascoarán Shayne." A live show turns **Héctor Belascoarán Shayne** into a subject, a contestant, a curiosity, maybe a suspect if the hour can twist hard enough. Television gets him first. Private detective work comes later.

That is the smart dirt under "Days in Combat." Héctor wants to solve a strangler case, but the episode keeps asking whether he is hunting the spectacle or feeding it. The premiere works best when the case becomes a performance trap.

## The Detective Is Born Under Bad Lighting

"Days in Combat" opens with a risky framing choice. Héctor does not enter as a polished investigator on the street, cigarette of destiny in hand, already certain of his myth. He appears on a live show, where his name becomes part of the event. That matters because the episode's central joke and central danger share the same source. Héctor has turned himself into a private detective after losing his old life, and the new one begins in public humiliation.

Héctor asks, "How did I end up a private detective making a fool of himself on TV?" The line does clean work. It gives the origin, admits the absurdity, and lets the show build a hero who understands how ridiculous he looks. The hour earns its noir flavor because it refuses to treat the detective fantasy as automatically cool. It puts the fantasy under studio lights and makes him sweat for it.

The live contest framing also gives the episode its cleanest engine. Crimes are ignored, many remain unsolved, and Héctor decides to use the public setup to chase a killer. Mexico City appears through institutional failure rather than postcard atmosphere. That is the sharper route. The danger comes through neglect: murders without answers, victims without closure, a killer who can turn indifference into oxygen.

## A Plumber, an Office, and the Price of Pretending

The episode's best grounding beat is **Gómez Letrás**, the plumber who confirms he is independent and trades the office setup with rules. It is a small scene in plot terms, but it gives the detective premise its working-class spine. Héctor's new identity is negotiated, borrowed, improvised. The office does not arrive as a shrine. It arrives through arrangement.

That choice keeps the show from floating into pure gimmick. Héctor can announce himself on television, but the practical world keeps tugging him back. He needs a place. He needs terms. He needs other people to accept, tolerate, or profit from the act he is putting on. Gómez Letrás makes the fantasy physical. An office has rules. Independence has a cost.

There is also a neat comic bite in the contrast between Héctor's declared mission and the scrappy mechanics around it. he says he will smoke out the strangler stalking Mexico City. Big sentence. Big promise. The hour then places that promise inside a structure that looks half official, half ridiculous. That is the episode's pulse: heroic intent traveling through shabby systems. When the writing trusts that contradiction, it has real flavor.

The flaw is that the office setup and the contest setup sometimes compete for control of the hour. Each frame is strong. Together, they create a slightly stop-start first stretch, as if the episode keeps recalibrating whether the main pleasure is procedural, satire, or origin story. The overlap is interesting. The rhythm wobbles.

## You Become the Bait

The episode's smartest tactical pivot comes when ordinary clue hunting gets rejected. The line "You become the bait" reframes the investigation from search to provocation. Héctor is trying to make the strangler look back.

That is where **Cerevro** becomes more than a name in the case file. The dossier marks him as someone who wants an audience and wants to be connected to the ongoing killings. He calls or frames Héctor for involvement, which turns the case into a mirror game. Héctor uses television to draw the killer out. Cerevro uses that same hunger for attention to pull Héctor into his design. The detective thinks he is controlling the stage. The killer understands there is a stage.

The host's "HE'LL RETURN!" announcement and the statement that a killer is at large in Mexico City sharpen the danger because they make murder part of broadcast momentum. The show inside the show does more than report the chase. It fuels it. Every return, every answer demanded from Héctor, every on-air escalation risks becoming useful to the person he wants to catch.

This is the episode's strongest argument. Publicity is not a tool Héctor can simply pick up and put down. Once he turns the case into a public contest, he cannot fully control who benefits from the attention. The spotlight can expose a killer and flatter him in the same breath.

## Paniagua's Threat Has a Crack in It

**Officer Paniagua** gives the premiere its clearest institutional contradiction. He wants Héctor to stop "playing pretend" and accept that the cases are already solved, while also threatening jail. Later, he is involved enough that Héctor is forced into negotiation and proof arrangements. That shift complicates the usual cop-versus-detective shape.

Paniagua could have been a simple obstacle, the official man telling the outsider to go home. The hour gives him a more useful function. His certainty looks less solid once the case keeps generating pressure. If everything is already solved, why does Héctor's proof matter? If Héctor is only pretending, why does the negotiation carry weight? The episode does not need Paniagua to deliver a speech about hypocrisy. His actions expose the gap.

The negotiation, with proof handed over and a warning of extortion, pulls the episode into darker procedural territory. The live-show energy has not disappeared, but by then the hour has shifted into longer pockets of silence and heavier momentum. That tonal move works because the case has earned a more serious register. The performance game is still there. The consequences have started to bruise.

The transition into those late beats is noticeable in a slightly mechanical way. The dossier's pacing pattern, quick contest dialogue early and long silences later, points to a deliberate contrast. It is effective, though not always elegant. The episode knows where it wants to land before it smooths the road there.

## The Girl with the Ponytail Turns the Case Human

The girl with the ponytail cuts through the episode's cleverness. Her mother was brutally murdered, and the murderer was never found. That beat matters because the hour has spent so much time with frames: the live show, the detective origin, the office bargain, the killer's attention games. Her story pulls the case away from format and back toward damage.

She also plants one of the premiere's key open loops. Who exactly is she, and how does her backstory connect to the strangler or stranglers? The episode does not answer that here, and the choice gives the season a wound rather than only a puzzle. Cerevro's misspelled name and the "lonely tree on a hill" riddle point toward a larger pattern, but the girl's grief gives that pattern a body.

This is where "Days in Combat" is at its most promising. The hour can be playful about Héctor's self-invention, funny about his public foolishness, and alert to the absurd bureaucracy around him. Then it can stop and let an unsolved murder sit in the room. The tonal swing is risky, but it keeps the episode from becoming detective cosplay. Héctor's performance may be messy. The victims are not props.

## The Verdict

"Days in Combat" is a strong, slightly uneven premiere built around a terrific contradiction: Héctor turns himself into bait on television, then discovers the killer may understand spectacle better than he does. The live-show framing gives the episode a distinct hook, Gómez Letrás grounds the detective fantasy in practical terms, and Paniagua's shifting posture gives the institutional conflict some bite. The girl with the ponytail adds the human cost the episode needs.

The craft is less clean when the early comic bustle gives way to late dark momentum, and the tonal gear change can be felt. Still, this is a confident opening hour with a real premise, useful messiness, and enough open loops to make the hunt worth following.

episode_reviews.title: No Happy Ending
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale case puts Belascoaran directly in the police's crosshairs when a corpse appears in his office. It is the most tightly wound of the three episodes and lands the series' running theme - that the system will punish anyone who actually does the work the system claims to want done.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The discovery of the planted body, which reframes everything Belascoaran thought he understood about who is actually in danger.
